studies.title: Spinorphin Ameliorates Nitroglycerin-Induced Migraine-Like Responses and Trigeminovascular Neuroinflammation Potentially Through Opioid Receptor-Mediated Mechanisms.
studies.authors: Demir, Cemalettin, Torun, Ibrahim Ethem, Baranoglu Kilinc, Yasemin, Kilinc, Erkan
studies.abstract: Enhancement of endogenous opioid signaling through inhibition of enkephalin degradation has emerged as a potential strategy for pain control, yet its role in migraine remains unclear. This study investigated whether spinorphin, an endogenous inhibitor of multiple enkephalinases, attenuates trigeminovascular activation and migraine-like responses in experimental migraine. Migraine-like pain was induced in male Wistar rats by nitroglycerin. The effects of spinorphin were evaluated using periorbital and plantar von Frey tests, followed by assessment of c-Fos levels in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) levels in the trigeminal ganglion (TG) and TNC, and meningeal mast cell degranulation. Opioid receptor involvement was examined using nalmefene. In complementary ex vivo hemiskull preparations, capsaicin-evoked CGRP release was quantified, and the interaction between spinorphin and sumatriptan was investigated. Spinorphin dose-dependently alleviated cephalic and extracephalic mechanical hypersensitivity, reduced c-Fos levels, decreased CGRP concentrations in the TG and TNC, and inhibited meningeal mast cell degranulation. These protective effects were markedly attenuated by nalmefene, supporting the involvement of opioid receptor-mediated mechanisms. In ex vivo preparations, spinorphin selectively reduced capsaicin-induced CGRP levels in the superfusates without affecting basal CGRP levels, and this effect was abolished by nalmefene. Moreover, spinorphin enhanced the inhibitory effect of sumatriptan on capsaicin-stimulated CGRP levels. Spinorphin attenuates behavioral, neurochemical, and neuroinflammatory features of experimental migraine, at least partly through mechanisms involving endogenous opioid signaling. These findings suggest enkephalinase inhibition as a promising therapeutic approach for migraine and support further investigation of spinorphin as a potential adjunct to established antimigraine therapies.

studies.title: Experimental Food Allergy: From Induction to Anaphylaxis Assessment in a Rat Model.
studies.authors: Reyes-Pavón, Diana, Jiménez, Mariela, Bermúdez-Humarán, Luis G, Salinas, Eva
studies.abstract: This chapter describes the experimental methodology used to establish a rat model of oral food allergy. The final protocol has been optimized for the Wistar strain. The model mimics chronic oral allergen re-exposure and allows the study of effector-phase allergic responses. It encompasses all experimental stages, including preliminary procedures, intramuscular sensitization, the use of pro-type 2 immune response adjuvants, allergen re-sensitization, and the final oral challenge, using ovalbumin (OVA). Key outcomes include clinical parameters such as sign scoring, diarrhea classification, and body temperature changes during oral anaphylaxis. In addition, immunological and inflammatory markers such as OVA-specific IgE titer, mast cell protease II, or even histamine can be assessed.

studies.title: PPARγ Activation Rescues High‑Fat Diet‑Induced Obesity Exacerbated Food Allergy by Maintaining Intestinal Homeostasis.
studies.authors: Yang, Fan, Liu, Yan, Zheng, Shuangyan, Meng, Xuanyi et al.
studies.abstract: High-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity has been suggested to be a potential risk factor for the increasing incidence of food allergies, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we investigated the causal role of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) in HFD-induced obesity exacerbated food allergy using both in vitro and in vivo approaches. In bone marrow‑derived mast cells (BMMCs), pharmacological inhibition of PPARγ enhanced IgE‑mediated degranulation and IL‑4 secretion without affecting IgE‑FcεRI binding, indicating that PPARγ negatively regulates mast cell activation independently of the initial receptor engagement. In HFD‑fed mice with ovalbumin‑induced food allergy, oral administration of the PPARγ agonist rosiglitazone alleviated allergic reactions by reducing mucosal mast cell activation, without significantly altering IgE levels. Mechanistically, PPARγ activation restored intestinal barrier integrity, expanded RORγt⁺ regulatory T cells in mesenteric lymph nodes, and reversed gut dysbiosis, particularly by restoring Ligilactobacillus abundance. Collectively, these findings establish that PPARγ suppression is a causal mediator of obesity‑exacerbated food allergy and highlight PPARγ as a potential target for preventive strategies against allergic disease in the context of obesogenic dietary patterns.

studies.title: Discovery of a Potent, Selective, and Orally Efficacious STAT6 PROTAC for the Treatment of Atopic Dermatitis.
studies.authors: Wang, Wentao, Zhao, Mengyu, Hu, Liuzhi, Wang, Chenxi et al.
studies.abstract: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6), a key mediator of IL-4/IL-13 signaling, regulates Th2 differentiation, making it an attractive target for atopic dermatitis (AD). The reported phosphopeptide-based STAT6 proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) established proof of concept for targeted STAT6 degradation, although its oral bioavailability and degradation potency remain suboptimal. Here, we report the discovery of orally active non-phosphopeptide STAT6 degraders. Among them, WW-210 exhibited picomolar DC50 values for STAT6 degradation and a more than 1000-fold degradation selectivity window over the other tested STAT family members. PK/PD studies demonstrated favorable oral exposure, measurable oral bioavailability, and effective STAT6 degradation in blood and spleen. In a mouse model of AD, WW-210 alleviated skin lesions, reduced serum IgE, restored filaggrin expression, and decreased mast cell infiltration. Collectively, WW-210 represents a potent, orally active STAT6 degrader with therapeutic potential for AD.

studies.title: Leveraging Structure-Based Design to Overcome Class III RTK Off-Target Activity in the Development of Selective Wild-Type KIT Inhibitors.
studies.authors: Moon, Hyunyoung, Yan, Xuelei, Zhu, Jiang, Mata, Guillaume et al.
studies.abstract: Selective KIT inhibition is an effective strategy for treating mast cell-driven diseases, but highly conserved ATP-binding sites in class III RTKs hinder selective inhibitor design. We employed structure-guided medicinal chemistry to optimize a series of potent, selective KIT inhibitors. An initial triazolopyridine hinge-binding motif enabled potent KIT inhibition with high selectivity and, after central linker optimization, led to a "reverse" arylacetamide series with further improved potency and pharmacokinetic properties. Incorporation of a pyrazole-based linker and modification of the hinge-binding motif led to improved potency in the presence of human serum. Further tuning of the terminal aryl substituent mitigated cytochrome P450 time-dependent inhibition and improved kinome selectivity. Crystallography revealed key elements of KIT inhibition and showed that subtle modulation of linker stereoelectronic effects in the gatekeeper region can drive selectivity. These efforts yielded an optimized lead inhibitor with low-nanomolar cellular potency, high KIT selectivity, and properties favorable for chronic therapy.

studies.title: Topical maltotetraose alleviates chronic pruritus by restoring skin barrier function and cutaneous homeostasis in C57BL/6J mice.
studies.authors: Gao, Fuqiang, Feng, Rong, Kong, Haocun, Tian, Yixiong et al.
studies.abstract: Food-grade ingredients are attracting increasing attention in cosmetic applications owing to their safety, biocompatibility, sustainability, and multifunctionality. Although maltotetraose (G4) has been reported to possess moisturizing and potential anti-pruritic properties, systematic in vivo evidence supporting its efficacy against chronic pruritus remains limited. Therefore, this study evaluated the anti-pruritic effects of topical G4 in an acetone-ether-water (AEW)-induced chronic pruritus mouse model and characterized the associated changes in skin barrier function, oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, neural-related signaling, and skin microbiota composition. G4 treatment significantly reduced scratching behavior and dermatitis severity while improving skin hydration and barrier function. These improvements were accompanied by enhanced expression of barrier-related proteins, increased antioxidant enzyme activities, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine levels, and decreased mast cell degranulation. G4 treatment was also associated with lower expression of itch-related transient receptor potential channels and substance P/neurokinin-1 receptor signaling markers, as well as reduced cutaneous nerve fiber density. Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed alterations in skin microbiota composition, including increased relative abundances of potentially beneficial taxa such as Adlercreutzia and Bifidobacterium and decreased abundance of Pseudomonas. Collectively, these findings suggest that G4 alleviates chronic pruritus in association with coordinated improvements in skin barrier function, inflammatory status, neural-related signaling, and microbiota composition, highlighting its potential as a food-derived ingredient for future skin health applications.

studies.title: Peanut-Specific IgG4 mAbs Promote Regulatory Immune Responses Ex Vivo and Improve Oral Immunotherapy in Mice.
studies.journal: Clinical and experimental allergy : journal of the British Society for Allergy and Clinical Immunology
studies.authors: Gasser, Pascal, Overman, Alex A J, Porbahaie, Mojtaba, Arena, Chiara et al.
studies.abstract: Peanut allergy remains a clinical challenge, with limited treatment options such as omalizumab (Xolair) and allergen immunotherapy (AIT). However, these are constrained by eligibility and safety concerns. AIT induces protective allergen-neutralizing IgG4 in most, but not all patients. Allergen-neutralizing IgG4 competes with allergen-specific IgE, inhibits FcεRI-mediated mast cell activation, and inhibits IgE-facilitated antigen presentation via CD23. Recent findings suggest that combining omalizumab with AIT enhances safety and reduces side effects. We hypothesize that controlled allergen exposure combined with peanut-specific IgG4 mAbs (MY-4-mAbs) prevents IgE binding to peanut allergens, reduces CD23-mediated allergen presentation and Th2 responses, and skews immunity towards protective allergen-specific IgG while limiting allergen-specific IgE induction. PBMCs from peanut-allergic donors were exposed to Ara h 2 with or without MY-4-mAbs. Th2 cytokines, Foxp3+ Tregs, and IgE-facilitated allergen binding (FAB) to B cells were assessed. In vivo, peanut-sensitized C3H/HeJ mice underwent oral-AIT with peanut extract with or without MY-4-mAbs and were monitored for anaphylaxis during and after oral-AIT. Additionally, peanut-specific IgG and IgE levels were measured before and after oral-AIT. Ex vivo, MY-4-mAbs with Ara h 2 suppressed Th2 cytokines, enhanced IL-10 secretion, and inhibited FAB. MY-4-mAbs redirected allergen binding to myeloid antigen-presenting cells and promoted tolerance-associated responses. In vivo, the combination maintained peanut-specific IgG induced during oral-AIT, prevented increases in IgE, and reduced mast cell activation. Allergen-specific IgG4 mAbs with controlled allergen exposure may improve the safety and efficacy of peanut AIT while promoting tolerance-associated immune responses, which might allow disease modification towards allergen tolerance.

studies.title: Mas-related G protein-coupled receptors contribute to compound 48/80-induced mast cell-independent activation of dorsal root ganglion neurons and itch in mice.
studies.authors: Shi, Ji, Wu, Dong-Ye, Sun, Shi-Yu, Liu, Tong et al.
studies.abstract: Compound 48/80 (C48/80) is widely used as a mast cell degranulator, and its pruritogenic action has generally been attributed to mast cell-derived mediators. Whether C48/80 also drives itch through a mast cell-independent neuronal mechanism remains unresolved. This study aimed to determine whether C48/80 evokes itch through direct, mast cell-independent activation of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory neurons and to identify the receptors involved. C48/80-evoked scratching was assessed in mice after resiniferatoxin (RTX)-mediated ablation of capsaicin-sensitive afferents, mast cell stabilization, antihistamine treatment, and in mast cell-deficient, transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (Trpa1 -/- ), and transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (Trpv1 -/- ) mice. Fura-2 ratiometric calcium imaging was performed in cultured primary DRG neurons to examine direct neuronal responses and the effects of TRPA1/TRPV1 deletion or Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor (MRGPR) blockade with Boc-Gln-D-Trp(Formyl)-Phe-OBzl (QWF). C48/80 evoked robust scratching in mice, and RTX-mediated ablation of capsaicin-sensitive afferents markedly reduced the number of scratch bouts. In contrast, cromolyn sodium or the antihistamine chlorpheniramine did not eliminate the response. C48/80 continued to elicit scratching in mast cell-deficient mice and produced comparable behavioral responses in Trpa1 -/- and Trpv1 -/- mice. In cultured primary DRG neurons, C48/80 evoked calcium responses that were not prevented by deletion of TRPA1 or TRPV1. By contrast, QWF, an MRGPR antagonist, strongly inhibited C48/80-induced calcium signaling and reduced scratch bouts after intraperitoneal administration. C48/80 can directly activate DRG neurons and induce itch through a mast cell-independent neuronal pathway. MRGPR-dependent signaling, rather than TRPA1 or TRPV1, is a key contributor to this direct neuronal component of C48/80-evoked itch.

studies.title: Cyanobacterium Brasilonema sp. LPS Induces Neutrophil Infiltration and Lung Inflammation in a TLR4-Dependent Manner and Exacerbates Th2-Dependent Lung Inflammation.
studies.authors: Swartzendruber, Julie, Toro, Rosalinda Monroy Del, Alfano, Peter, Incrocci, Ryan et al.
studies.abstract: Chronic airway inflammation can be induced by both chemical and environmental factors. Airway inflammation can be induced through different immune pathways, including allergic Th2-dependent activation of eosinophils and mast cells, Th1/Th17-dependent neutrophil recruitment, or a combination of both mast cell and neutrophil recruitment, that is extremely difficult to treat. An environmental factor that we have shown to induce neutrophil-mediated lung inflammation is cyanobacterium lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The study has two main objectives: first to determine whether TLR4 is required for cyanobacterium LPS-induced lung inflammation, given our prior findings that it signals differently from other LPS types, and second to test if cyanobacterium LPS exacerbates lung inflammation in a Th2-dependent mouse model of airway hypersensitivity. LPS from the cyanobacterium strain, Brasilonema sp., was purified and used for both in vivo and in vitro assays. For in vitro assays, the TLR4 inhibitor, SPA-4, was assessed in its ability to block Brasilonema sp.-dependent IL-6 and IL-8 induction in lung epithelial cell lines, and in vivo, the ability of Brasilonema sp. LPS to induce lung inflammation was assessed in TLR4-deficient mice in comparison to controls. Finally, Th2-driven lung inflammation was established using ovalbumin and then these mice were exposed to Brasilonema sp. LPS intranasally to assess if Brasilonema sp. LPS resulted in the exacerbation of Th2-dependent airway inflammation. Our results indicate that Brasilonema sp. LPS stimulates the production of cytokines both in vitro and in vivo in a TLR4-dependent manner, since the addition of the SPA-4 peptide blocks Brasilonema sp. LPS-dependent increases in IL-6 and IL-8 in vitro and TLR4-deficient mice were refractory to Brasilonema sp. LPS-mediated induction of lung inflammation in vivo. Additionally, both E. coli and Brasilonema sp. LPS exacerbated airway inflammation in a Th2-dependent model of lung inflammation. However, Brasilonema sp. LPS exacerbated Th2-dependent lung inflammation without significant neutrophil infiltration. Despite the altered signaling through TLR4 by cyanobacterium LPS, these data demonstrate that lung inflammation induced by LPS from the cyanobacterium strain, Brasilonema sp., requires TLR4 and exacerbates Th2-dependent lung inflammation. Therefore, novel interventions that target TLR4 may be beneficial in the treatment of LPS-induced lung inflammation from environmental exposure.

studies.title: Hypermobility spectrum disorder/hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, mast cell activation syndrome, and dysautonomia as risk factors for adverse events and complications.
studies.authors: Blitshteyn, Svetlana, Sivakoti, Kirti, Afrin, Lawrence B
studies.abstract: Hypermobility spectrum disorder/hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (HSD/hEDS), mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), and dysautonomia, including postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), are comorbid conditions encountered in clinical practice with possible overlapping immunologic, autonomic, and connective tissue abnormalities. Clinicians frequently observe that individuals affected with these syndromes commonly experience disproportionate adverse events and complications from a variety of stressors. We review clinical observations and emerging evidence via PubMed on adverse events and complications experienced by patients with HSD/hEDS, MCAS, and dysautonomia in response to surgery, postoperative period, anesthesia, medication side effects, substance sensitivities, and infection. Patients with HSD/hEDS, MCAS, and dysautonomia may be at a higher risk of adverse events and complications associated with surgery, medication, substances, and infection. Recognition and awareness of these syndromes and possible risks, which each disorder may carry alone or as a triad, can lead to risk mitigation, appropriate counseling, and prognostication. Future studies should focus on longitudinal multicenter studies assessing risks and outcomes in this vulnerable patient population. Translational studies are also needed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying adverse events and complications in patients with HSD/hEDS, MCAS, and dysautonomia.

studies.title: Anesthesia Considerations for Transfemoral Osseointegration in a Patient With CRPS, Propofol, and Ketamine Allergies: A Case Report.
studies.authors: Fanizza, Jake D, Hoellwarth, Jason Shih, Umeh, Uchenna O
studies.abstract: A 20-year-old female with asthma, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, mast cell activation syndrome, and complex regional pain syndrome Type 1 (CRPS1) presented for left transfemoral amputation with osseointegration and nerve reconstruction. To limit CRPS1 exacerbation, neuraxial anesthesia with femoral and sciatic blocks was administered for analgesia. Given the reported history of convulsions following ketamine and propofol, sedation with midazolam, dexmedetomidine, and fentanyl was used. On POD 1, fascia iliaca and sciatic blocks were repeated to mitigate postoperative pain. There were no intraoperative or postoperative complications. With limited literature on anesthesia for osseointegration, this novel case highlights individualized planning, in the setting of adverse responses to anesthetic medications and challenging pain management.

studies.title: A Case of Suspected Scombroid Poisoning in Intensive Care Staff: Is It Anaphylaxis?
studies.authors: Hamilton, William, Ivatt, Helen, Cartwright, Gwendolen
studies.abstract: Scombroid poisoning (histamine fish poisoning) is an uncommon foodborne illness that frequently mimics immunoglobulin E-mediated anaphylaxis. We report a case of a previously well 28-year-old intensive care nurse who developed abrupt facial flushing, wheeze, dizziness, and hypotension after consuming canned tuna. Initial observations demonstrated sinus tachycardia and hypotension. She was treated according to established anaphylaxis guidelines with two doses of intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, and subsequent adrenaline infusion in intensive care. She recovered rapidly and was discharged the following day. Serial serum mast cell tryptase measurements at approximately one hour, six hours, and 24 hours after symptom onset were all within normal limits. In the absence of previous allergy history and given the temporal association with tuna ingestion, scombroid poisoning was considered as a possible diagnosis. This case highlights the difficulty of distinguishing severe histamine fish poisoning from anaphylaxis in the acute setting and reinforces that life-threatening presentations should initially be managed according to anaphylaxis protocols until an alternative diagnosis can be established.

studies.title: Case Report: Histamine-mediated inflammation and mast cell modulation in central serous chorioretinopathy: a two case illustrations.
studies.authors: KamaliZonouzi, Sara, Babaei Zadeh, Parsa, Popovic, Marko M, Gorin, Michael B et al.
studies.abstract: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is characterized by retinal pigment epithelium dysfunction and choroidal hyperpermeability. Beyond established associations such as psychosocial stress and corticosteroid exposure, experimental and epidemiological findings raise the possibility that mast cell and histamine-related pathways may contribute to CSCR pathophysiology. This study reviews mechanistic and clinical evidence for the role of histamine in the pathogenesis of CSCR, as well as the role of histamine-targeted therapies in this condition. We also present two cases, highlighting the possible therapeutic role of anti-allergy agents in CSCR. We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL to October 2025 for studies of antihistamines and/or mast-cell stabilizers, alone or in combination in central serous retinopathy and pachychoroid spectrum diseases. Eligible designs included human observational and controlled studies. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and appraised data using ROBINS-I, NOS, and GRADE. Results were narratively synthesized. After screening 316 articles, three studies (430 patients, 390 controls) from India and the United States were included. Direct evidence for anti-allergy therapeutics was limited to a single management series, in which short-course antihistamine treatment showed no meaningful visual or anatomical benefit; however, improvements occurred spontaneously or after focal laser. One case-control study reported a higher prevalence of antihistamine use and allergic disorders among CSCR patients (OR 4.1), suggesting a possible histamine-mediated risk. Another case-control study found no statistically significant association between antihistamine use and CSCR after multivariable adjustment. Analysis of the literature revealed inconsistent associations between antihistamine use and CSCR risk, with a brief therapeutic trial offering no benefit for acute CSCR. However, two illustrative cases demonstrate temporal associations between interruption of anti-allergic therapy and subsequent CSCR activity, followed by anatomical improvement after treatment re-initiation or modification. These observations are hypothesis-generating but cannot establish therapeutic efficacy or causality, particularly given concurrent treatment changes in case 1. Given the inconclusive therapeutic data, further randomized controlled trials are warranted to more rigorously evaluate sustained mast-cell stabilization regimens before drawing clinical conclusions.

studies.title: Sodium Alginate Modification as a Promising Strategy for Inducing Oral Immune Tolerance to Fish Gelatin-Based Cell Scaffolds to Control Allergenic Risks.
studies.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
studies.authors: Wang, Shuya, Shi, Mengqing, Li, Ya, Qin, Lei et al.
studies.abstract: The allergenic risks of fish gelatin-based cell scaffolds remain an unresolved issue. The study proposed a sodium alginate modification strategy to solve allergenic risks by inducing oral immune tolerance. The strategy significantly reduced antibody production, mast cell degranulation, inflammatory mediator release, and Th2 immune response. Peptidomics and bioinformatics prediction revealed that the strategy protected CD4+ T cell epitopes (FTGASGLPG) and CD8+ T cell epitopes (e.g., GATGPTGL). Additionally, intestinal barrier function, integrity, and Th1/Th2/Th17/Treg immune balance were restored. Notably, compared with the positive control group, RORγt expression was suppressed by 73.42%, and FOXP3 expression was increased by 5.34-fold in the 1% group. Gut microbiota analysis suggested that sodium alginate modification significantly downregulated the abundance of Faecalibaculum and Lactobacillus, while increasing Prevotella. It regulates the intestinal microbiota, thereby contributing to immune tolerance induction. Overall, sodium alginate modification represents a promising strategy to promote immune tolerance.

studies.title: Nutritional strategies to manage postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and its comorbidities: A narrative review.
studies.authors: Kokorelis, Christina, Heyman, Andrea, Rowe, Peter C
studies.abstract: BackgroundPostural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) is a heterogeneous disorder of the autonomic nervous system characterized by orthostatic intolerance and involvement of multiple organ systems. It commonly coexists with conditions such as hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), and a spectrum of gastrointestinal (GI) disorders. These overlapping conditions frequently manifest with shared GI symptoms such as nausea, bloating, abdominal pain, early satiety, and altered bowel habits that can substantially compromise nutritional status and quality of life.AimThis review synthesizes current evidence to outline practical, nutrition-based strategies for managing POTS and its commonly associated comorbidities.MethodsKey nutritional domains relevant to POTS management, including fluid and sodium intake, meal timing and volume, and dietary composition, along with commonly associated comorbid conditions contributing to GI symptom burden, were identified a priori by the authors. These comorbidities include gastroparesis, hEDS, MCAS, disordered eating patterns, median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS), functional GI disorders, and food intolerances. A comprehensive PubMed search was then performed to identify and synthesize relevant literature within each of these predefined domains.SummaryGiven the clinical heterogeneity of POTS and variability in associated conditions, a standardized dietary approach is unlikely to be effective. Instead, individualized nutrition strategies tailored to symptom patterns, GI tolerance, metabolic demands, and co-existing disorders are essential. Careful evaluation of overlapping comorbidities is critical to inform targeted, sustainable, and patient-centered dietary management.

studies.title: Type 2 Inflammation in Chronic Spontaneous Urticaria: Presentation, Role, and Management.
studies.authors: Makris, Michael, Papapostolou, Niki, Koumprentziotis, Ioannis-Alexios, Gregoriou, Stamatis
studies.abstract: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a heterogeneous inflammatory skin disease characterized by recurrent wheals, angioedema, and pruritus, with substantial effects on quality of life. Although mast-cell activation remains the central effector event, increasing evidence implicates type 2 inflammatory pathways in CSU and suggests that the disease shares biological features with established type 2 inflammatory disorders, including atopic dermatitis, asthma, chronic prurigo, and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. This review examines the contribution of type 2 inflammation to CSU, its relationship with established autoimmune endotypes, associated biomarkers, and implications for current and emerging therapies. Type 2 cytokines, including IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and IL-31, together with epithelial alarmins and neuroimmune pathways, interact with IgE-dependent, autoimmune, and other mechanisms to amplify mast-cell activation, inflammation, and pruritus. Importantly, type 2 inflammation should not be regarded as an alternative to the established type I autoallergic/type IIb autoimmune classification, but rather as a partly overlapping and variably expressed inflammatory axis. No validated biomarker currently defines a type 2-high CSU endotype or reliably guides individual treatment selection; total IgE, eosinophils, basophils, autoantibodies, and functional basophil assays provide complementary mechanistic or prognostic information but remain insufficient for precision prescribing. The expanding therapeutic landscape reflects this biological complexity. Omalizumab targets IgE-dependent activation, dupilumab directly inhibits IL-4/IL-13 signaling, whereas BTK inhibitors such as remibrutinib interfere with intracellular mast-cell and basophil signaling across multiple upstream mechanisms. Emerging KIT-directed therapies extend this strategy through direct targeting of the mast-cell compartment. Nevertheless, heterogeneous cytokine signatures and variable therapeutic responses argue against defining CSU as a uniformly type 2-driven disease. Future progress will require prospectively validated biomarker signatures, biomarker-stratified trials, comparative studies of emerging therapies, and long-term evaluation of treatment-free remission and potential disease modification. Defining the contribution and boundaries of type 2 inflammation within the broader pathobiology of CSU may ultimately facilitate the transition from mechanistic understanding to clinically actionable precision medicine in CSU.

studies.title: CD300f acts as an inducible inhibitory checkpoint that limits mast cell activation by suppressing MITF-dependent activation.
studies.authors: Song, Lihong, Ollé, Laia, Zhang, Zeng, Lago, Natalia et al.
studies.abstract: Mast cells (MCs) are key regulators of cutaneous immune responses and play a central role in allergic and non-IgE-mediated skin inflammation by activating the Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2). The inhibitory receptor CD300f has been shown to modulate MC activation, but its role in regulating MRGPRX2-dependent signaling remains unclear. Here, we investigated CD300f expression and function in human skin MCs and its impact on MRGPRX2-mediated responses, with some comparison to IgE-mediated responses. CD300f was expressed on human skin MCs, and its surface expression increased following MRGPRX2 activation. Engagement of CD300f significantly attenuated MC activation induced by MRGPRX2-dependent stimuli, including substance P, vancomycin, and quinolone drugs. Transcriptomic analyses in CD300f-LAD2 revealed that CD300f signaling suppressed activation-associated gene programs after substance P stimulation, including NF-κB and MAPK pathways. Notably, CD300f engagement markedly downregulated microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF), as confirmed at the protein level in LAD2 and skin MCs. MITF inhibition with TT012 and CD300f triggering enhance inhibitory responses, decreasing MITF and MITF-target expression more strongly. Conversely, lysyl-tRNA synthetase overexpression increases MITF expression and significantly reduces CD300f-mediated inhibition of both MRGPRX2- and FcεRI-dependent signaling. These findings reveal a CD300f-MITF regulatory axis that limits skin MC activation and inflammatory responses.

studies.title: Genetically engineering mast cells as effectors for targeted cancer cell cytotoxicity.
studies.authors: Han, Xiao, Wen, Di, Fu, Ruxing, Soto, Jennifer et al.
studies.abstract: Type-I hypersensitivity is a mast cell-mediated degranulation process induced by IgE-antigen recognition. Inspired by this highly specific mechanism, we developed a new cell therapy platform by genetically engineering mouse mast cell line MC/9 to overexpress the cytotoxic proteins perforin and granzyme B (PG-MCs) via lentiviral transduction. In the melanoma model utilizing B16 cells expressing membrane-bound OVA, a polarized degranulation of mast cells towards cancer cells was validated upon the recognition of antigens by anti-OVA IgE. PG-MCs could selectively kill cancer cells via IgE-antigen recognition. The IgE-sensitized PG-MCs administered through an intertumoral route delivered perforin 1 (Prf1) and granzyme B (Gmzb) toward target cells to potentiate anti-tumor efficacy. Moreover, we demonstrated the reprogramming effect of tumor microenvironment by PG-MC-induced hypersensitivity, driving an immune remodeling of the tumor milieu, characterized by the increased lymphocyte infiltration. In addition, this mast cell therapy, in combination with 5- fluorouracil (5-Fu), induced a significant inhibition of tumor growth in a B16-OVA mouse model, which is associated with the depletion of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs).

studies.title: Thiophene-Benzimidazole Conjugates Attenuate IL-33-induced Inflammation in Human Mast Cell Line and in ex vivo Human Skin Organ Cultures.
studies.authors: Gvirtz, Raanan, Kahremany, Shirin, Trifonov, Lena, Weintraub, Sagiv et al.
studies.abstract: Aberrant Interleukin-33 (IL-33) activation is associated with numerous dermatological inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as atopic dermatitis, lupus, vitiligo and psoriasis. Thus, the inhibition of this pathway may provide therapeutic options in multiple pathologies. We hypothesized that targeting the IL-33 critical site of interactions with its membranal receptor, Suppression of Tumorigenicity 2 (ST2), will generate highly selective inhibitors capable of alleviating the detrimental effects of IL-33 activation. In silico-based methods for the identification of possible inhibitors of IL-33/ST2 interaction were used. Employing two structure-based pharmacophore models designed by LigandScout, a virtual screening of commercially available compounds and in house library revealed 13 compounds that may reduce level of IL-33/ST2 interaction. To verify their capacity to attenuate IL-33-induced inflammation, the compounds were tested in HMC-1.1 mast cell line and human skin slices. Two lead compounds, both thiophene-benzimidazole conjugates methyl-1-(pentan-3-yl)-2-(thiophen-2-ylmethyl)-1H-benzo[d]imidazole-5-carboxylate (LT-105) and methyl (S)-5-methyl-3-{(1-(pentan-3-yl)-2-(thiophen-2-ylmethyl)-1H-benzo[d]imidazole-5-carboxamido)}hexanoate (LT-108), were able to attenuate IL-33-induced IL-6 and IL 8 hypersecretion in pharmacological relevant concentrations. This effect correlated with reduced IL-6 and IL-8 mRNA levels, determined by RT-PCR. In addition, LT-105 and LT-108 reduced the phosphorylation of IL-33 downstream effectors; p-IRAK1 and p-P38. Further docking studies revealed possible molecular interactions of the compounds with key sites of IL-33 that are responsible for the binding with ST2. To validate the findings, the compounds were also tested in the ex vivo human skin organ culture. Both compounds LT-105 and LT-108 reduced inflammation when applied topically to the human skin samples stimulated by IL-33 in pharmacological concentrations. Our results indicate that thiophene-benzimidazole conjugates LT-105 and LT-108 can reduce IL-33 mediated inflammation both in vitro and ex vivo. Nevertheless, additional in vivo and clinical studies are required to further evaluate the ability of these compounds to treat autoimmune/inflammatory cutaneous disorders mediated by IL-33.

studies.title: Topical Remibrutinib Attenuates LL37-Induced Rosacea-Like Dermatitis by Inhibiting BTK Activation, NF-κB Signaling and Mast Cell Activation.
studies.authors: Li, Wangchao, Fan, Huiping, Liu, Hua, Ma, Qingsong et al.
studies.abstract: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder in which LL37-driven mast cell activation contributes to cutaneous inflammation. Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) is a key regulator of canonical IgE-dependent mast cell responses; however, its role in LL37-induced, IgE-independent mast cell activation remains unclear. This study investigated the involvement of BTK activation and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling in LL37-induced mast cell activation and evaluated the therapeutic effects of topical remibrutinib in experimental rosacea-like dermatitis. Transcriptomic data from rosacea lesions (GSE65914) were analyzed to identify dysregulated inflammatory pathways. LL37-stimulated LUVA mast cells and an LL37-induced mouse model of rosacea-like dermatitis were used for in vitro and in vivo evaluation, respectively. Cell viability, mast cell degranulation, and inflammatory mediator production were assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay (CCK-8) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA). Cutaneous inflammation and dermal mast cell accumulation were evaluated by histopathological examination and toluidine blue staining. BTK and NF-κB phosphorylation were examined by Western blotting and immunofluorescence. Consistently, gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated enrichment of the NF-κB signaling pathway, with BTK included among the leading-edge genes contributing to this transcriptional signature. LL37 increased BTK and p65 phosphorylation in LUVA cells and mouse skin, accompanied by enhanced mast cell degranulation and inflammatory mediator release. Topical treatment with 1% remibrutinib reduced BTK and p65 phosphorylation, mast cell accumulation and degranulation, and inflammatory mediator levels. These changes were accompanied by reductions in erythema, epidermal thickening, and histopathological inflammation in mice. BTK and NF-κB are involved in LL37-induced, IgE-independent mast cell activation and rosacea-like inflammation. Topical remibrutinib attenuated experimental rosacea-like dermatitis by inhibiting BTK phosphorylation and NF-κB activation and mast cell activation, supporting topical BTK inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for rosacea.

studies.title: Phenotyping Interstitial Cystitis/Bladder Pain Syndrome: Clinical and Mechanistic Evidence, Candidate Biomarkers, and Implications for Management.
studies.authors: Qiao, Pengfei, Tian, Zhentao, He, Zhen
studies.abstract: Interstitial cystitis and bladder pain syndrome are clinically overlapping conditions that should be distinguished according to Hunner lesion status. IC with Hunner lesions is a distinct inflammatory bladder disease characterized by urothelial denudation, lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, adaptive immune activation, and progressive structural impairment. The intensity and distribution of these inflammatory and structural abnormalities may vary among patients with IC, but the underlying pathological pattern is comparatively coherent. BPS without Hunner lesions is substantially more heterogeneous. Urothelial barrier dysfunction, mast cell and sensory nerve signaling, pelvic floor dysfunction, peripheral sensitization, and central or nociplastic pain mechanisms may contribute to symptoms in different combinations. Candidate urine and blood-based biomarkers, including cytokines, chemokines, neurotrophic factors, immune cell indices, and multiomics signatures, may support phenotyping, assessment of disease activity, or prediction of treatment response. However, most remain exploratory because their intended clinical use, analytical standardization, diagnostic thresholds, and external validity have not been established. This narrative review compares the clinical and histopathological features of IC and BPS, evaluates the evidence for proposed immune and neuroregulatory mechanisms, examines the translational status of candidate biomarkers, and discusses disease-specific and phenotype-guided management. These findings support a primary distinction between IC and BPS. Additional phenotyping is useful after this distinction to characterize heterogeneity within BPS and clinically relevant coexisting mechanisms.

studies.title: A Review: Mast Cells as Targets for Glucocorticoid Action.
studies.authors: Atum, Daniel, Ogwal, Jimmy Odongo, Obeny, Abel
studies.abstract: This review aims to summarize the established and potential targets of glucocorticoids (GCs) on mast cells, which are implicated in the pathophysiology of various allergic and inflammatory diseases including asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis. We sought to answer the following questions: (1) How do glucocorticoids inhibit the release of mediators from mast cells? (2) What are the effects of glucocorticoids on mast cell signaling molecules? (3) By what mechanisms do glucocorticoids induce mast cell apoptosis? and (4) What are the genomic and non-genomic mechanisms underlying these effects? Evidence published since 2020 reinforces that glucocorticoid effects on mast cells are context dependent rather than uniform. Dexamethasone can directly suppress selected functions of human and murine mast cells, including in combination with inhibitory CD300a signaling [22]. Conversely, activated human lung mast cells can reduce corticosteroid responsiveness in neighboring airway smooth muscle cells by altering glucocorticoid-regulated transcription [23]. In patients with asthma, six weeks of inhaled budesonide reduced airway mast cell infiltration and improved airway hyperresponsiveness; importantly, associations differed according to mast cell phenotype, airway location, and inflammatory phenotype [25]. Single-cell studies now reveal multiple human mast cell transcriptional states across tissues [7, 8], while integrated RNA-seq and H3K27ac profiling in primary human mast cells demonstrates selective regulation of mast-cell identity genes and super-enhancer networks [92]. These findings place glucocorticoid responsiveness within a framework of mast cell state, tissue niche, species, glucocorticoid compound, and experimental context. Glucocorticoid-associated mast cell depletion may involve reduced stromal/fibroblast-derived SCF and, in IL-3-dependent murine models, reduced IL-3 receptor expression; these are mechanistically distinct effects. Glucocorticoids can target mast cells at several levels, including mediator synthesis and release, intracellular signaling, survival, and transcriptional regulation, but the magnitude and nature of these effects vary substantially among species, tissue compartments, mast cell phenotypes/states, glucocorticoid compounds, activation pathways, and experimental conditions. Classical GR-dependent transcription involves GRE-dependent regulation and interactions with transcription factors such as NF-κB and AP-1, yet mast-cell-specific GR-regulated gene and chromatin programs remain incompletely defined. Rapid effects on degranulation are also unresolved, with evidence for membrane-associated classical GR signaling as well as other rapid mechanisms. Contemporary human and single-cell data therefore argue against treating mast cells as a single uniformly corticosteroid-responsive population. Future studies should define the molecular basis of rapid glucocorticoid signaling and map GR-responsive transcriptional and chromatin programs across primary human mast cell states and tissue niches.
